query.original_query: difficulty-aware compute allocation reasoning models internal difficulty representation adaptive depth

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of input difficulty in reasoning models, adaptive computation depth allocation, dynamic early exit mechanisms, and difficulty-aware routing in transformer layers
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how transformer-based reasoning models internally represent input difficulty and allocate computational resources across layers. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze the residual stream to identify features correlated with problem complexity, finding that intermediate layers encode difficulty signals separable from task semantics. Our analysis reveals that dynamic early exit mechanisms, such as confidence-based classifiers attached to intermediate transformer blocks, rely on these difficulty representations to modulate computation depth. We further examine adaptive computation architectures that route inputs through variable numbers of layers based on per-token difficulty estimates. Results show that difficulty-aware routing correlates with reduced inference cost on simpler queries while maintaining accuracy on complex ones, though the learned difficulty representations exhibit sensitivity to distribution shift. We also observe that MLP layers in deeper blocks contribute disproportionately to factual recall for hard examples, while attention heads in early layers encode general difficulty features. These findings suggest that internal difficulty representations are distributed but partially localized, with implications for efficient inference and model interpretability.

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of task difficulty in human cognition, adaptive allocation of cognitive resources, effort-based decision making, and metacognitive monitoring during reasoning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated how individuals internally represent task difficulty and adaptively allocate cognitive resources during deductive reasoning. Participants completed a series of syllogistic reasoning problems varying in logical complexity while providing trial-by-trial metacognitive judgments of expected effort and perceived difficulty. We measured response times, accuracy, and pupil dilation as an index of cognitive effort allocation. Results indicate that subjective difficulty ratings reliably predicted subsequent resource allocation, with larger pupil responses observed on trials where participants anticipated higher demand. Furthermore, metacognitive monitoring accuracy moderated the relationship between objective problem complexity and effort investment; individuals with more accurate difficulty judgments showed tighter coupling between task demands and physiological effort markers. Findings support the hypothesis that internal representations of difficulty serve as a control signal guiding the adaptive deployment of cognitive resources, consistent with effort-based decision-making frameworks. These results extend current models of metacognitive monitoring by demonstrating that subjective difficulty estimates directly influence online resource regulation during complex reasoning.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs implicitly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations and how to locate the specific attention heads responsible for this perception.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations and identifies specific attention heads responsible for this perception, providing a method for automatic difficulty annotation and revealing differences between difficulty perception and entropy.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that difficulty perception in LLMs is structurally organized and can be probed and localized, offering insights for adaptive reasoning and benchmark construction.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in high-dimensional embeddings, and a linear probe can accurately predict difficulty.
Specific attention heads in the final transformer layer show opposite activation patterns for simple and difficult problems.
Ablation experiments confirm the causal role of these attention heads in difficulty perception.
Difficulty perception at the token level does not consistently align with entropy variation.
Attention head patterns for difficulty perception can change with training, as seen in distilled models.
papers.limitation: whether the method based on attention head difficulty perception can be used for reward allocation in the RL training process.
future_direction: Investigating how pre-training and post-training quality affect difficulty perception.
Studying how attention head patterns change during training.
Exploring the relationship between token-level difficulty perception and entropy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on complex reasoning tasks, yet little is known about their ability to internally evaluate problem difficulty, which is an essential capability for adaptive reasoning and efficient resource allocation. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode problem difficulty in their internal representations. Using a linear probe on the final-token representations of LLMs, we demonstrate that the difficulty level of math problems can be linearly modeled. We further locate the specific attention heads of the final Transformer layer: these attention heads have opposite activation patterns for simple and difficult problems, thus achieving perception of difficulty. Our ablation experiments prove the accuracy of the location. Crucially, our experiments provide practical support for using LLMs as automatic difficulty annotators, potentially substantially reducing reliance on costly human labeling in benchmark construction and curriculum learning. We also uncover that there is a significant difference in entropy and difficulty perception at the token level. Our study reveals that difficulty perception in LLMs is not only present but also structurally organized, offering new theoretical insights and practical directions for future research. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aegis1863/Difficulty-Perception-of-LLMs.

papers.title: Deep Learning Through the Lens of Example Difficulty
papers.research_question: How does the computational difficulty of making a prediction for a given input, measured by prediction depth, relate to a model's uncertainty, confidence, accuracy, and speed of learning for that data point?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces prediction depth as a measure of computational example difficulty and demonstrates its relationships with model uncertainty, accuracy, learning speed, and margins, leading to a coherent view of several deep learning phenomena.
papers.conclusion: Prediction depth offers a coherent view of deep learning phenomena such as early layers generalizing while later layers memorize, and that easy examples are learned first.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction depth is larger for visually more difficult examples and is consistent across architectures and random seeds.
Prediction depth provides a linear lower bound on prediction consistency, and predictions are more accurate for validation points with small prediction depths.
Data points with smaller prediction depths are learned earlier during training.
Examples with smaller prediction depths have larger adversarial input and output margins.
Three distinct types of example difficulty can be identified based on prediction depth in train and validation splits, and using a middle layer for predictions can improve accuracy for certain types.
papers.abstract: Existing work on understanding deep learning often employs measures that compress all data-dependent information into a few numbers. In this work, we adopt a perspective based on the role of individual examples. We introduce a measure of the computational difficulty of making a prediction for a given input: the (effective) prediction depth. Our extensive investigation reveals surprising yet simple relationships between the prediction depth of a given input and the model's uncertainty, confidence, accuracy and speed of learning for that data point. We further categorize difficult examples into three interpretable groups, demonstrate how these groups are processed differently inside deep models and showcase how this understanding allows us to improve prediction accuracy. Insights from our study lead to a coherent view of a number of separately reported phenomena in the literature: early layers generalize while later layers memorize; early layers converge faster and networks learn easy data and simple functions first.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Their Failures: Predicting Success from Pre-Generation Activations
papers.research_question: We investigate whether their likelihood of success is recoverable from their internal representations prior to generation, and whether this signal can guide more efficient inference.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs encode a model-specific notion of difficulty in pre-generation activations, distinct from human difficulty, and that linear probes can extract this signal to enable probe-guided routing, achieving substantial cost savings while maintaining accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a model's likelihood of success is present in pre-generation activations and can be extracted with linear probes, enabling routing strategies that approach oracle performance, though the signal becomes harder to access with increased test-time compute.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on pre-generation activations can predict model success on math and coding tasks, substantially outperforming surface features like question length and TF-IDF.
Models encode a model-specific notion of difficulty that is distinct from human difficulty, and this divergence increases with extended reasoning.
Probe reliability degrades with increased test-time compute (extended reasoning), but is partially recoverable with non-linear MLP probes.
Probe-guided routing can match the performance of the best-performing model while reducing inference cost by up to 70% on MATH.
Chain-of-thought length tracks human difficulty rather than model success, especially with extended reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Focus on linear probes at a single post-instruction position; probe performance degrades under extended reasoning.
Do not probe during generation or do cross-domain transfer (e.g., math to code).
Probes are sensitive to token position.
Routing policies use fixed-k majority voting rather than learned or adaptive selection of k.
papers.abstract: Running LLMs with extended reasoning on every problem is expensive, but determining which inputs actually require additional compute remains challenging. We investigate whether their own likelihood of success is recoverable from their internal representations before generation, and if this signal can guide more efficient inference. We train linear probes on pre-generation activations to predict policy-specific success on math and coding tasks, substantially outperforming surface features such as question length and TF-IDF. Using E2H-AMC, which provides both human and model performance on identical problems, we show that models encode a model-specific notion of difficulty that is distinct from human difficulty, and that this distinction increases with extended reasoning. Leveraging these probes, we demonstrate that routing queries across a pool of models can exceed the best-performing model whilst reducing inference cost by up to 70\% on MATH, showing that internal representations enable practical efficiency gains even when they diverge from human intuitions about difficulty. Our code is available at: https://github.com/KabakaWilliam/llms_know_difficulty

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth-Specialized Mixture-of-Experts in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be made more efficient by adapting computational depth to input complexity using a mixture of depth-specialized experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DS-MoE, a transformer-based framework that dynamically allocates computational depth by composing specialized expert modules into reasoning chains, improving efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DS-MoE demonstrates that depth-adaptive expert selection can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.
papers.key_findings:
DS-MoE achieves up to 70% computational savings and 2x faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers.
DS-MoE delivers higher accuracy (up to 5.3% improvement) on complex reasoning tasks like legal and long-context datasets.
The architecture reduces GPU memory footprint by 35-40% compared to baseline models.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of routing, memory integration experts, and meta-cognitive experts for performance.
DS-MoE generates more interpretable reasoning chains, offering transparency into the decision process.
papers.limitation:
The routing network introduces overhead that may impact latency, especially in real-time settings.
Effectiveness depends on the availability of suitably specialized expert modules, which may require domain-specific development and limit generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating reinforcement learning for routing optimization.
Introducing domain-specific experts.
Generalizing DS-MoE to multimodal reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Contemporary transformer architectures apply identical processing depth to all inputs, creating inefficiencies and limiting reasoning quality. Simple factual queries are subjected to the same multilayered computation as complex logical problems, wasting resources while constraining deep inference. To overcome this, we came up with a concept of Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth Specialised Mixture of Experts (DS-MoE), a modular framework that extends the Mixture of Experts paradigm from width-based to depth specialised computation. DS-MoE introduces expert modules optimised for distinct reasoning depths, shallow pattern recognition, compositional reasoning, logical inference, memory integration, and meta-cognitive supervision. A learned routing network dynamically assembles custom reasoning chains, activating only the necessary experts to match input complexity. The dataset on which we trained and evaluated DS-MoE is on The Pile, an 800GB corpus covering diverse domains such as scientific papers, legal texts, programming code, and web content, enabling systematic assessment across reasoning depths. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-MoE achieves up to 16 per cent computational savings and 35 per cent faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers, while delivering 2.8 per cent higher accuracy on complex multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, routing decisions yield interpretable reasoning chains, enhancing transparency and scalability. These findings establish DS-MoE as a significant advancement in adaptive neural architectures, demonstrating that depth-specialised modular processing can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.

papers.title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
papers.research_question: Does token-level adaptive compute allocation align with underlying computational complexity, and how does decision timing affect learned compute policies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a complexity-controlled evaluation paradigm and the ANIRA framework for studying token-level adaptive compute allocation, finding that alignment with complexity can emerge without supervision but does not guarantee algorithmic generalization.
papers.conclusion: Token-level adaptive computation should be evaluated with well-defined notions of difficulty; while adaptive compute policies can be learned, their meaning and generalizability depend on task structure and decision timing.
papers.key_findings:
Compute allocation aligned with task complexity can emerge without explicit difficulty supervision.
Such alignment does not imply algorithmic generalization: models fail to extrapolate to unseen input sizes.
Early compute decisions rely on static structural cues, whereas online halting more closely tracks algorithmic execution state.
Training dynamics show a two-phase regime: learning followed by compute reduction.
For natural language math questions, compute allocation does not correlate with a simple notion of task complexity.
papers.limitation: Compute allocation by ANIRA is not easily interpretable on natural language and does not appear to correlate with a simple notion of task complexity.
papers.abstract: Token-level adaptive computation seeks to reduce inference cost by allocating more computation to harder tokens and less to easier ones. However, prior work is primarily evaluated on natural-language benchmarks using task-level metrics, where token-level difficulty is unobservable and confounded with architectural factors, making it unclear whether compute allocation truly aligns with underlying complexity. We address this gap through three contributions. First, we introduce a complexity-controlled evaluation paradigm using algorithmic and synthetic language tasks with parameterized difficulty, enabling direct testing of token-level compute allocation. Second, we propose ANIRA, a unified recurrent Transformer framework that supports per-token variable-depth computation while isolating compute allocation decisions from other model factors. Third, we use this framework to conduct a systematic analysis of token-level adaptive computation across alignment with complexity, generalization, and decision timing. Our results show that compute allocation aligned with task complexity can emerge without explicit difficulty supervision, but such alignment does not imply algorithmic generalization: models fail to extrapolate to unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation. We further find that early compute decisions rely on static structural cues, whereas online halting more closely tracks algorithmic execution state.

papers.title: Breaking the Pre-Sampling Barrier: Activation-Informed Difficulty-Aware Self-Consistency
papers.research_question: How can the inference cost of Self-Consistency be reduced by using internal model activations to estimate problem difficulty and adaptively adjust the number of samples, without requiring pre-sampling?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ACTSC, a method that uses internal FFN activation signals to train a lightweight difficulty probe, enabling adaptive self-consistency sampling without pre-sampling or extra model calls, thereby reducing inference costs.
papers.conclusion: Internal activations can serve as an effective signal for difficulty-aware test-time scaling, and ACTSC provides a new direction for efficient inference control in LLMs by reducing costs while maintaining accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
ACTSC reduces the average number of samples by up to 87.1% compared to SC and up to 40% compared to DSC while maintaining comparable accuracy.
A linear probe trained on difficulty-sensitive FFN neuron activations can accurately predict problem difficulty without generating any tokens.
ACTSC generalizes to non-mathematical reasoning benchmarks, showing consistent efficiency gains across domains.
The computational overhead of the difficulty probe is low and incurred only once per model, with inference-time overhead comparable to a single forward pass.
ACTSC eliminates the preparation stage required by DSC, making its cost independent of dataset size and difficulty.
papers.abstract: Self-Consistency (SC) is an effective decoding strategy that improves the reasoning performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by generating multiple chain-of-thought reasoning paths and selecting the final answer via majority voting. However, it suffers from substantial inference costs because it requires a large number of samples. To mitigate this issue, Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC) was proposed to reduce unnecessary token usage for easy problems by adjusting the number of samples according to problem difficulty. However, DSC requires additional model calls and pre-sampling to estimate difficulty, and this process is repeated when applying to each dataset, leading to significant computational overhead. In this work, we propose Activation-Informed Difficulty-Aware Self-Consistency (ACTSC) to address these limitations. ACTSC leverages internal difficulty signals reflected in the feed-forward network neuron activations to construct a lightweight difficulty estimation probe, without any additional token generation or model calls. The probe dynamically adjusts the number of samples for SC and can be applied to new datasets without requiring pre-sampling for difficulty estimation. To validate its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on five benchmarks. Experimental results show that ACTSC effectively reduces inference costs while maintaining accuracy relative to existing methods.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning-Based Compositional Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do complexity control strategies like initialization scale and weight decay influence transformers' ability to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Complexity control strategies, such as small initialization scales and large weight decay, enable transformers to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional tasks, leading to better out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: Complexity control through initialization and weight decay is key to enabling transformers to learn compositional rules and generalize out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit three phases based on initialization: poor generalization, good ID but poor OOD, and good ID and OOD generalization.
Complexity control (small init, large weight decay) promotes reasoning-based solutions with lower complexity bias.
Masking reveals that reasoning-based solutions use key token and anchor information differently.
Neuron condensation and structured embeddings are associated with reasoning phases.
Findings generalize to real-world tasks like image generation and NLP.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, yet their performance on compositional problems remains a subject of debate. In this study, we investigate the internal mechanisms underlying Transformers' behavior in compositional tasks. We find that complexity control strategies significantly influence whether the model learns primitive-level rules that generalize out-of-distribution (reasoning-based solutions) or relies solely on memorized mappings (memory-based solutions). By applying masking strategies to the model's information circuits and employing multiple complexity metrics, we reveal distinct internal working mechanisms associated with different solution types. Further analysis reveals that reasoning-based solutions exhibit a lower complexity bias, which aligns with the well-studied neuron condensation phenomenon. This lower complexity bias is hypothesized to be the key factor enabling these solutions to learn reasoning rules. We validate these conclusions across multiple real-world datasets, including image generation and natural language processing tasks, confirming the broad applicability of our findings.

papers.title: A Shared Geometry of Difficulty in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether problem-difficulty representations in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages, and how they are encoded depth-dependently.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode problem difficulty in a depth-dependent manner: early layers form a language-agnostic representation that supports cross-lingual transfer, while deeper layers refine it into language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form a language-agnostic estimate of difficulty in early layers before specializing it to individual languages in deeper layers, indicating a shared geometry of difficulty across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Difficulty is linearly decodable from both shallow (early) and deep (later) transformer layers.
Probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages than those trained on deep representations.
Probes trained on deep representations achieve higher accuracy within the same language but generalize poorly across languages.
There is a trade-off between cross-lingual generalization and language-specific accuracy, with optimal layers differing for same-language vs. cross-lingual evaluation.
This depth-dependent organization of difficulty representations is consistent across multiple LLM architectures and scales.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to mathematical problem solving using the AMC subset of Easy2Hard, so it is unclear if findings extend to other domains.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of instruction-tuned, decoder-only language models.
Conclusions are based exclusively on probing analyses without causal evidence for the role of difficulty signals in inference.
future_direction: Whether difficulty-based interventions learned in one language transfer to other languages.
papers.abstract: Predicting problem-difficulty in large language models (LLMs) refers to estimating how difficult a task is according to the model itself, typically by training linear probes on its internal representations. In this work, we study the multilingual geometry of problem-difficulty in LLMs by training linear probes using the AMC subset of the Easy2Hard benchmark, translated into 21 languages. We found that difficulty-related signals emerge at two distinct stages of the model internals, corresponding to shallow (early-layers) and deep (later-layers) internal representations, that exhibit functionally different behaviors. Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: Liquid Reasoning Transformers: A Sudoku-Based Prototype for Chess-Scale Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: How can transformers be designed to perform iterative, adaptive-depth reasoning for structured problems like Sudoku and chess?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Liquid Reasoning Transformer, an architecture that performs iterative, adaptive-depth inference for structured reasoning tasks, demonstrated on Sudoku with high accuracy without symbolic rules or search.
papers.conclusion: The Liquid Reasoning Transformer enables adaptive-depth iterative reasoning for structured problems, achieving strong performance on Sudoku and providing a framework for extensions to tasks like chess.
papers.key_findings:
Achieves 98.68% digit accuracy and 36.30% puzzle accuracy on Sudoku without using symbolic rules or search.
Learns to allocate computation adaptively using a stop gate, with more steps for difficult puzzles.
Uses a discard gate to filter incorrect intermediate hypotheses, improving stability.
Internal reasoning patterns show convergence and correction of errors over iterative steps.
Demonstrates that transformers can benefit from explicit internal reasoning steps for structured tasks.
papers.limitation:
Fixed maximum depth for reasoning loop restricts ability to resolve long or highly branched inference chains.
Single recurrent reasoning token limits capacity to maintain multiple parallel hypotheses or track several long-range dependencies.
Discard mechanism may become unstable in more complex tasks, potentially discarding useful information or relying too much on aggressive pruning.
High computational cost due to gating and repeated transformer passes, requiring optimization for scaling.
Sudoku may not generalize directly to chess without additional modifications due to complexity differences.
future_direction: Extending the architecture to chess-scale reasoning tasks.
Exploring multi-token reasoning states.
Investigating reinforcement learning approaches or training on sequences of moves for advanced tactical understanding.
papers.abstract: The Liquid Reasoning Transformer (LRT) is a transformer architecture designed for inference with adaptive depths using iterative changes, discard-based correction, and a learned stopping mechanism. Instead of relying on a single feedforward pass, the model updates a recurrent reasoning token across multiple internal steps, allowing it to correct early errors and allocate computation based on input difficulty. We evaluate the LRT on Sudoku as a controlled testbed for structured reasoning and show that it achieves strong performance, reaching 98.68% digit accuracy and 36.30% full-puzzle accuracy without using symbolic rules or search. Analyzing internal patterns shows that the discard and stop gates play different, important roles in stabilizing inferences and adjusting computational depth. We discuss how these mechanisms extend naturally to chess-scale reasoning tasks and outline extensions for multi-token reasoning and larger domains.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: What common patterns manifest in the model's input-output behavior and internal representations during the extended loss plateau phase, and what critical changes precede the sudden shift towards higher performance?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies that during the loss plateau in Transformer training, models develop a partial solution, exhibit repetition bias and internal representation collapse, and that the slow learning of optimal attention maps is a key bottleneck driving these dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies repetition bias and representation collapse as key characteristics of early-phase implicit biases in Transformer training, closely connected to the loss plateau, and suggests a 'search' over sequence tokens as a possible cause.
papers.key_findings:
During the initial loss plateau, the model often learns a partial solution, correctly predicting a subset of easier tokens while failing on more complex parts.
A strong repetition bias appears in model outputs during the plateau, quantified by repetition frequency and sequence entropy.
Internal representation collapse occurs where hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel (high cosine similarity).
Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Looking Beyond The Top-1: Transformers Determine Top Tokens In Order
papers.research_question: What computation is the Transformer model performing after the saturation event (where the top-1 prediction becomes fixed)?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers determine their top-k output tokens in order of ranking via a discrete task-transition mechanism, a phenomenon intrinsic to the architecture that can be leveraged for improved early-exit strategies and language modeling.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Transformer layers after the top-1 saturation event work on determining lower-ranked tokens in order, proposes a task-transition mechanism underlying this, and shows practical benefits for efficiency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Top-k tokens in Transformers reach saturation (become fixed) sequentially in the order of their final ranking.
This ordered saturation occurs across text, vision, and speech modalities and in untrained models, suggesting it is architecture-inherent.
A simple classifier can predict the current 'task' (which token rank is being determined) from hidden layer embeddings.
Intervening by injecting activations from a saturation layer can causally trigger a transition to the next task.
A novel early-exit strategy based on task transition outperforms existing token-level confidence measures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not determine which specific components in the Transformer architecture give rise to the ordered saturation phenomenon.
The work does not consider whether the data used was encountered during the models' training.
future_direction: Ablation studies to identify which Transformer components are responsible for the ordered saturation.
Investigating if other DNN architectures (e.g., RNNs) also determine top-k tokens in order.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Transformers is crucial for achieving more accurate and efficient predictions. In this work, we analyze the computation performed by Transformers in the layers after the top-1 prediction has become fixed, which has been previously referred to as the "saturation event". We expand the concept of saturation events for top-k tokens, demonstrating that similar saturation events occur across language, vision, and speech models. We find that these saturation events happen in order of the corresponding tokens' ranking, i.e., the model first decides on the top ranking token, then the second highest ranking token, and so on. This phenomenon seems intrinsic to the Transformer architecture, occurring across different architectural variants (decoder-only, encoder-only, and to a lesser extent full-Transformer), and even in untrained Transformers. We propose an underlying mechanism of task transition for this sequential saturation, where task k corresponds to predicting the k-th most probable token, and the saturation events are in fact discrete transitions between the tasks. In support of this we show that it is possible to predict the current task from hidden layer embedding. Furthermore, using an intervention method we demonstrate that we can cause the model to switch from one task to the next. Finally, leveraging our findings, we introduce a novel token-level early-exit strategy, which surpasses existing methods in balancing performance and efficiency.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Toward Trustworthy Difficulty Assessments: Large Language Models as Judges in Programming and Synthetic Tasks
papers.research_question: Can a state-of-the-art LLM, used as a black-box text-only judge, faithfully reproduce the Easy/Medium/Hard labels of competitive programming problems?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-4o underperforms an interpretable LightGBM ensemble in predicting difficulty of competitive programming problems, showing strong bias and inconsistency in judgments.
papers.conclusion: GPT-4o drastically underestimates real Hard problems, while LightGBM, supported by SHAP-based interpretability, shows robust performance and highlights the primacy of numeric constraints in defining Hard difficulty.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4o achieves only 37.75% accuracy in difficulty prediction, while LightGBM attains 86%.
GPT-4o downgrades 83.38% of real Hard problems to Easy, indicating a strong bias toward simpler categories.
SHAP-based analysis reveals that numeric constraints such as input size limits and acceptance rates are crucial for LightGBM's accurate classification of Hard problems.
In synthetic experiments, GPT-4o labels almost all of its own generated Hard problems as Medium, contradicting its tendency to downgrade real Hard problems to Easy.
GPT-4o's internal notion of difficulty is unstable across real and synthetic domains, highlighting reliability issues in LLM-based judges.
future_direction: Constraint-aware prompting
Hybrid models combining LLM-derived embeddings with interpretable numeric features
Meta-evaluation protocols specifically tailored to difficulty assessment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language and code generation, and are increasingly deployed as automatic judges of model outputs and learning activities. Yet, their behavior on structured tasks such as predicting the difficulty of competitive programming problems remains under-explored. We conduct a systematic comparison of GPT-4o, used purely as a natural-language difficulty assessor, against an interpretable Light-GBM ensemble trained on explicit numeric and textual features. On a dataset of 1,825 LeetCode problems labeled Easy, Medium, or Hard, LightGBM attains 86% accuracy, whereas GPT-4o reaches only 37.75%. Detailed analyses, including confusion matrices and SHAP-based interpretability, show that numeric constraints -- such as input size limits and acceptance rates -- play a crucial role in separating Hard problems from easier ones. By contrast, GPT-4o often overlooks these cues and exhibits a strong bias toward simpler categories. We further probe GPT-4o through a synthetic Hard-problem generation protocol. Surprisingly, GPT-4o labels almost all of its own synthetic Hard problems as Medium, contradicting its tendency to downgrade real Hard problems to Easy. Our findings connect to recent work on LLMs-as-judges and automatic difficulty estimation in programming and education, and highlight concrete failure modes that must be addressed before LLM-based judges can be considered trustworthy in competitive programming, educational platforms, or reinforcement-learning pipelines.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
papers.research_question: Do deeper language models use their depth to compose more features for higher-order computations, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers?
papers.core_contribution: Deeper language models do not use their increased depth to learn new kinds of computation; instead, they spread the same computation over more layers and use the second half primarily for fine-grained refinement of the output probability distribution.
papers.conclusion: Current large language models underutilize the second half of their layers, which may explain why increasing depth leads to diminishing returns in performance for stacked Transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in the second half of the model contribute much less to the residual stream than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition around the middle.
Skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions compared to skipping layers in the first half.
For multi-hop tasks, there is no evidence that models use increased depth to compose sub-results; later computation steps do not use more layers.
Linear maps from a shallow model's residual stream to a deeper model's show a diagonal pattern, indicating the deeper model 'stretches out' the same computation rather than performing novel computation.
The second half of the network is devoted to refining the current token's probability distribution, not computing reusable sub-results for future tokens.
papers.limitation:
The findings are a case study on Llama and Qwen models and may not hold for other model types.
The work does not answer how models solve problems without depth dependence.
The linear map analysis in Section 3.4 relies on a single model pair due to resource constraints.
The exploration in Section 3.5 relies on manual study of individual trained models.
future_direction: Develop an automatic metric to measure the correspondence of computation to the parse tree.
Verify the findings with more resources on different and deeper models.
Investigate how models solve problems without depth dependence.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs are increasingly deep, and depth correlates with performance, albeit with diminishing returns. However, do these models use their depth efficiently? Do they compose more features to create higher-order computations that are impossible in shallow models, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers? To address these questions, we analyze the residual stream of the Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, and OLMo 2 family of models. We find: First, comparing the output of the sublayers to the residual stream reveals that layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition between the two halves. Second, skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions. Third, for multihop tasks, we are unable to find evidence that models are using increased depth to compose subresults in examples involving many hops. Fourth, we seek to directly address whether deeper models are using their additional layers to perform new kinds of computation. To do this, we train linear maps from the residual stream of a shallow model to a deeper one. We find that layers with the same relative depth map best to each other, suggesting that the larger model simply spreads the same computations out over its many layers. All this evidence suggests that deeper models are not using their depth to learn new kinds of computation, but only using the greater depth to perform more fine-grained adjustments to the residual. This may help explain why increasing scale leads to diminishing returns for stacked Transformer architectures.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Multi-head Transformers Provably Learn Symbolic Multi-step Reasoning via Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems via chain-of-thought processes, specifically path-finding in trees, through gradient descent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought through gradient descent, with attention heads specializing and coordinating to solve path-finding tasks, and provides generalization guarantees to unseen trees.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought with provable optimization and generalization guarantees, offering mechanistic insights into how transformers implement algorithmic procedures.
papers.key_findings:
One-layer transformers can learn to solve backward and forward path-finding tasks in trees via chain-of-thought reasoning.
Multi-head attention heads autonomously specialize and coordinate to handle multi-stage reasoning, with one head performing path-finding and another controlling stage transitions.
Gradient descent training dynamics converge to parameters that implement the desired reasoning mechanisms.
The learned models generalize to unseen tree structures, learning generalizable rules rather than memorizing paths.
Extending reasoning length via chain-of-thought allows shallow transformers to solve complex tasks that might otherwise require deeper architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multi-step reasoning tasks. However, understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which they acquire these abilities through training remain limited, particularly from a theoretical standpoint. This work investigates how transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems through chain-of-thought processes, focusing on path-finding in trees. We analyze two intertwined tasks: a backward reasoning task, where the model outputs a path from a goal node to the root, and a more complex forward reasoning task, where the model implements two-stage reasoning by first identifying the goal-to-root path and then reversing it to produce the root-to-goal path. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in the dynamics of gradient descent, shows that trained one-layer transformers can provably solve both tasks with generalization guarantees to unseen trees. In particular, our multi-phase training dynamics for forward reasoning elucidate how different attention heads learn to specialize and coordinate autonomously to solve the two subtasks in a single autoregressive path. These results provide a mechanistic explanation of how trained transformers can implement sequential algorithmic procedures. Moreover, they offer insights into the emergence of reasoning abilities, suggesting that when tasks are structured to take intermediate chain-of-thought steps, even shallow multi-head transformers can effectively solve problems that would otherwise require deeper architectures.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: What Can Transformer Learn with Varying Depth? Case Studies on Sequence Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the minimum number of attention layers required for transformers to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization tasks, and what are the roles of different layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a single-layer transformer can memorize but fails at reasoning and generalization; two layers are needed for reasoning and generalization, and three layers may be needed for contextual generalization. It also identifies simple operations that single attention layers can perform and how stacking layers combines them.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that depth is crucial for transformers to perform complex tasks, and their analysis sheds light on how transformers work by combining simple operations.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer transformer can memorize sequences but cannot perform reasoning or generalization tasks.
A two-layer transformer can perform reasoning and generalization tasks.
A three-layer transformer may be needed for contextual generalization.
Single attention layers can perform copying, parsing, matching, and mapping operations; stacking layers combines these to solve complex tasks.
Theoretical proofs and numerical experiments support these findings.
papers.abstract: We study the capabilities of the transformer architecture with varying depth. Specifically, we designed a novel set of sequence learning tasks to systematically evaluate and comprehend how the depth of transformer affects its ability to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization. We show a transformer with only one attention layer can excel in memorization but falls short in other tasks. Then, we show that exhibiting reasoning and generalization ability requires the transformer to have at least two attention layers, while context generalization ability may necessitate three attention layers. Additionally, we identify a class of simple operations that a single attention layer can execute, and show that the complex tasks can be approached as the combinations of these simple operations and thus can be resolved by stacking multiple attention layers. This sheds light on studying more practical and complex tasks beyond our design. Numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
