We call this the "weights component", and the remainder is identified as the "context component". By conducting meticulous and controlled experiments on synthetic tasks, we note that the persistence of learning plateaus correlates with compromised functionality of the weights component. Recognizing the impaired performance of the weights component as a fundamental behavior drives learning plateaus, we have developed three strategies to expedite the learning of Transformers. The effectiveness of these strategies is further confirmed in natural language processing tasks. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the feasibility of cultivating a powerful in-context learning ability within AI systems in an eco-friendly manner.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Knee-Deep in C-RASP: A Transformer Depth Hierarchy
papers.research_question: What capabilities are gained by increasing the depth of transformers? Specifically, what languages can be expressed by transformers of various depths?
papers.core_contribution: Proves a strict depth hierarchy for fixed-precision transformers (and with positional encodings) by showing equivalence to temporal logic TL[#←] and using a depth hierarchy in the logic.
papers.conclusion: Deeper transformers are more expressive, and the depth hierarchy predicts the difficulty of learning sequential dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
Fixed-precision transformers (without rounding inside attention) are expressively equivalent to TL[#←] and this equivalence preserves depth.
There is a strict depth hierarchy for TL[#←], meaning deeper formulas can express languages that shallower formulas cannot.
Consequently, fixed-precision transformers have a strict depth hierarchy: deeper transformers can recognize languages (like L_{k+1}) that shallower transformers cannot.
The same depth hierarchy holds for transformers with sinusoidal positional encodings, RoPE, and ALiBi.
Empirical results show that the depth required to learn L_k matches the theoretical predictions.
papers.abstract: It has been observed that transformers with greater depth (that is, more layers) have more capabilities, but can we establish formally which capabilities are gained? We answer this question with a theoretical proof followed by an empirical study. First, we consider transformers that round to fixed precision except inside attention. We show that this subclass of transformers is expressively equivalent to the programming language C-RASP and this equivalence preserves depth. Second, we prove that deeper C-RASP programs are more expressive than shallower C-RASP programs, implying that deeper transformers are more expressive than shallower transformers (within the subclass mentioned above). The same is also proven for transformers with positional encodings (like RoPE and ALiBi). These results are established by studying a temporal logic with counting operators equivalent to C-RASP. Finally, we provide empirical evidence that our theory predicts the depth required for transformers without positional encodings to length-generalize on a family of sequential dependency tasks.

papers.title: Allocation of Parameters in Transformers
papers.research_question: How should the model parameters – mainly attention heads and head dimensions – be allocated across Transformer layers to balance expressivity and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis and experimental validation to derive principled strategies for allocating attention heads and head dimensions across Transformer layers, improving model efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for parameter allocation in Transformers and offers practical guidelines for designing efficient architectures.
papers.key_findings:
There is a trade-off between the number of attention heads and head dimensions for information extraction in early layers, given a fixed parameter budget.
Softmax activations exhibit a saturation pattern where increasing head dimensions yields diminishing returns, especially for long sequences, enabling parameter reduction in later layers.
Principled parameter allocation strategies can be formulated based on the approximation error estimate and the softmax saturation behavior.
Numerical experiments on tasks like 4-gram modeling and head compression validate the theoretical trade-offs and saturation patterns.
The proposed allocation strategies can guide the design of more parameter-efficient Transformer architectures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on single-layer and shallow Transformers; extending it to deep architectures and more complex tasks is an important future direction.
The proposed strategies require validation in large-scale pretraining and transfer learning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deep Transformer architectures and more complex tasks.
Exploring alternative attention mechanisms and their interactions with feed-forward modules and optimization.
Validating the allocation strategies in large-scale pretraining and transfer learning to reduce computation and memory costs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved remarkable successes across a wide range of applications, yet the theoretical foundation of their model efficiency remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate how the model parameters -- mainly attention heads and head dimensions -- should be allocated across layers to balance expressivity and efficiency. We first provide mathematical analysis on the role of early layers in information extraction from an approximation perspective, with a theoretical characterization on the trade-off between the number of heads and head dimension under a fixed parameter budget. In addition, we uncover and prove the \emph{saturation} behavior of softmax activations: Continuously increasing head dimensions can lead to diminishing returns in learning errors, particularly for long sequences. Supported by both theory and experiments, this saturation pattern suggests that later layers can operate more efficiently with reduced parameters. Combining these insights, we propose principled strategies for allocating attention heads and dimensions across Transformers' layers, shedding light on theoretically-grounded model efficiency of Transformer-based architectures.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation
papers.research_question: How to leverage concept vectors to build logical implication into pre-trained transformer models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments to induce generation behavior in response to concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS) method, which uses concept vectors to program logical implication into pre-trained transformer models for interpretable behavior steering.
papers.conclusion: LIMS unlocks new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
LIMS improves performance on hallucination detection, unanswerable question rejection, adversarial safety, and math reasoning tasks.
LIMS works effectively in low-data regimes (e.g., with 100 training examples).
LIMS outperforms 10-shot prompting and has advantages over DPO in interpretability and resource usage.
The method is interpretable, allowing decoupled analysis of sensing and steering components.
Mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) performs similarly to LIMS with easier deployment but slightly reduced interpretability.
papers.limitation: The mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) variant reduces interpretability slightly compared to standard LIMS.
future_direction: Exploring LIMS across different models or modalities.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability in pre-trained transformer models has demonstrated substantial evidence supporting the ''linear representation hypothesis'', which is the idea that high level concepts are encoded as vectors in the space of activations of a model. Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept's vector to the corresponding activations. We show how to leverage these properties to build a form of logical implication into models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments that induce a chosen generation behavior in response to the presence of any given concept. Our method, Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS), unlocks new hand engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Duo-LLM: A Framework for Studying Adaptive Computation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically study adaptive computation in LLMs to identify optimal routing patterns for dynamic token processing based on complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Duo-LLM framework for studying adaptive computation in LLMs, uses oracles to identify optimal routing patterns, defines token difficulty, and shows the gap between oracle and learned routers.
papers.conclusion: The Duo-LLM framework is effective for understanding adaptive computation dynamics, revealing a gap between oracle and learned routers, and suggests future work on surrogate metrics and methods to avoid exhaustive enumeration for practical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Oracle routing achieves lower perplexity than random or fixed patterns and can identify configurations where activating only one big layer per token outperforms using big layers across all layers.
When compute budget is limited, later layers are prioritized; when budget is high, earlier layers get more compute.
Token difficulty is relative and some tokens do not benefit from additional compute, indicating that loss alone is not a reliable indicator of need for compute.
Learned routers are suboptimal compared to oracle and show different routing patterns, such as favoring later layers and early exits.
Training Duo-LLM from scratch outperforms freezing the big module and only training the small modules.
papers.limitation:
The oracle requires exhaustive iteration over all possible options, which is computationally demanding and time-intensive.
Computing the oracle's loss requires access to ground truth labels, making it impractical for real-world deployment.
future_direction: Develop surrogate metrics that eliminate the need for ground truth loss.
Devise methods that bypass the exhaustive enumeration of all options.
Bridge the performance gap between router training in conventional MoEs and the oracle.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) typically generate outputs token by token using a fixed compute budget, leading to inefficient resource utilization. To address this shortcoming, recent advancements in mixture of expert (MoE) models, speculative decoding, and early exit strategies leverage the insight that computational demands can vary significantly based on the complexity and nature of the input. However, identifying optimal routing patterns for dynamic execution remains an open challenge, limiting the full potential of these adaptive methods. To address this need, we study adaptive computation in LLMs more systematically. We propose a novel framework that integrates smaller auxiliary modules within each Feed-Forward Network layer of the LLM. This design enables dynamic routing of tokens based on task complexity: tokens can be processed by either the small or big modules at each layer, or even bypass certain layers entirely. This allows us to introduce a novel notion of a token's difficulty, defined by its potential to benefit from additional computational resources. Importantly, by employing oracles to identify optimal patterns of adaptive computations, we gain valuable insights into the internal workings of LLMs and the routing processes in a simplified heterogeneous MoE setup. We show that trained routers operate differently from oracles and often yield suboptimal solutions. Notably, activating a large module in just one layer outperforms models that use large modules across all layers, underscoring the gap between practical implementations of routing in MoE models and theoretical optima for adaptive computation.

papers.title: The Kinetics of Reasoning: How Chain-of-Thought Shapes Learning in Transformers?
papers.research_question: How does chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision affect the learning dynamics and generalization of transformers on formal reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT supervision accelerates generalization in transformers on certain reasoning tasks and can be modeled by a kinetic framework, but it also reveals a transient phase of unfaithfulness where answers are correct but reasoning traces are not.
papers.conclusion: CoT supervision advances the take-off point and often raises the ceiling of generalization, but it also reveals a transient faithfulness gap. Mechanistic analyses show that CoT shifts computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
CoT generally improves task performance but its benefits depend on task complexity.
CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections.
There is a transient trace unfaithfulness phase where models produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps.
CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically, shifting computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
Learning curves for both CoT and non-CoT training can be described by a predictable logistic function in log training steps.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic reasoning tasks used are different from real-world reasoning tasks, and the setup does not assess how natural language understanding (i.e., large-scale pretraining) affects CoT reasoning.
The study uses a fixed-size transformer architecture; extending the study to different model sizes could provide more insights on whether model scale affects the learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision can substantially improve transformer performance, yet the mechanisms by which models learn to follow and benefit from CoT remain poorly understood. We investigate these learning dynamics through the lens of grokking by pretraining transformers on symbolic reasoning tasks with tunable algorithmic complexity and controllable data composition to study their generalization. Models were trained under two settings: (i) producing only final answers, and (ii) emitting explicit CoT traces before answering. Our results show that while CoT generally improves task performance, its benefits depend on task complexity. To quantify these effects, we model the accuracy of the logarithmic training steps with a three-parameter logistic curve, revealing how the learning speed and shape vary with task complexity, data distribution, and the presence of CoT supervision. We also uncover a transient trace unfaithfulness phase: early in training, models often produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps, before later aligning their reasoning traces with answers. Empirically, we (1) demonstrate that CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections; (2) introduce a kinetic modeling framework for understanding transformer learning; (3) characterize trace faithfulness as a dynamic property that emerges over training; and (4) show CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically.

papers.title: Learning to Skip the Middle Layers of Transformers
papers.research_question: Can a Transformer architecture that dynamically skips middle layers, guided by interpretability insights about layer redundancy, improve the trade-off between language modeling performance and computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel Transformer architecture with a learned gating mechanism to dynamically skip a variable number of middle layers, aiming to reduce compute for simpler tokens. However, at the scales investigated, it does not improve the validation cross-entropy vs. estimated FLOPs trade-off compared to dense baselines with fewer layers.
papers.conclusion: At the small scales investigated, the proposed architecture did not yield improvements in the performance-efficiency trade-off. The anticipated benefits may only become apparent at significantly larger model scales where middle-layer redundancy is more pronounced.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed gated architecture did not improve the cross-entropy vs. FLOPs trade-off compared to dense baseline models with fewer layers.
Without controlling the sparsity of the gates, the mean sparsity tends toward zero and gated models perform similarly to dense baselines.
With sparsity control, increasing sparsity reduces estimated FLOPs but does not yield better performance than simply using a dense model with fewer layers.
The 'sandwich' or 'peri-layernorm' scheme was used to control residual norms in the architecture with skip connections.
An adaptive regularization loss was used to control the sparsity of the gate values, with a proportional update rule performing best among alternatives.
papers.limitation: The architecture did not improve the trade-off between validation cross-entropy and estimated FLOPs at the scales investigated.
future_direction: Investigating the architecture at significantly larger model scales where the redundancy of middle layers is more pronounced and the relative overhead of the gating mechanism is smaller.
papers.abstract: Conditional computation is a popular strategy to make Transformers more efficient. Existing methods often target individual modules (e.g., mixture-of-experts layers) or skip layers independently of one another. However, interpretability research has demonstrated that the middle layers of Transformers exhibit greater redundancy, and that early layers aggregate information into token positions. Guided by these insights, we propose a novel architecture that dynamically skips a variable number of layers from the middle outward. In particular, a learned gating mechanism determines whether to bypass a symmetric span of central blocks based on the input, and a gated attention mechanism prevents subsequent tokens from attending to skipped token positions. Residual norms are controlled with a 'sandwich' or 'perilayernorm' scheme and gate sparsity with an adaptive regularization loss. We had aimed to reduce compute requirements for 'simpler' tokens and potentially foster an emergent multi-level representational hierarchy but, at the scales investigated, our approach does not achieve improvements in the trade-off between validation cross-entropy and estimated FLOPs compared to dense baselines with fewer layers. We release our code at https://github.com/tim-lawson/skip-middle.

papers.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of transformer LLMs on compositional tasks, and are their errors incidental or do they signal fundamental limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks via linearized subgraph matching rather than systematic reasoning, and they exhibit exponential error accumulation with increased complexity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers have inherent limitations in solving compositionally complex tasks, and fundamental innovations are needed to address these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers' accuracy on compositional tasks drops to near zero as task complexity increases.
Fine-tuning on task-specific data leads to near-perfect in-domain performance but poor out-of-domain generalization.
Transformers learn surface patterns (e.g., via relative information gain) rather than underlying algorithms.
Correct predictions correlate with frequency of subgraph patterns in training data, indicating pattern matching.
Error analysis shows propagation errors dominate, indicating failure to compose steps.
papers.limitation: Due to budget constraints, grokking experiments were only conducted on the multiplication task.
future_direction: Using transformers for tasks decomposable into few reasoning steps
Using transformers in combination with planning modules or refinement methods
Fundamental innovations to address limitations
papers.abstract: Transformer large language models (LLMs) have sparked admiration for their exceptional performance on tasks that demand intricate multi-step reasoning. Yet, these models simultaneously show failures on surprisingly trivial problems. This begs the question: Are these errors incidental, or do they signal more substantial limitations? In an attempt to demystify transformer LLMs, we investigate the limits of these models across three representative compositional tasks -- multi-digit multiplication, logic grid puzzles, and a classic dynamic programming problem. These tasks require breaking problems down into sub-steps and synthesizing these steps into a precise answer. We formulate compositional tasks as computation graphs to systematically quantify the level of complexity, and break down reasoning steps into intermediate sub-procedures. Our empirical findings suggest that transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks by reducing multi-step compositional reasoning into linearized subgraph matching, without necessarily developing systematic problem-solving skills. To round off our empirical study, we provide theoretical arguments on abstract multi-step reasoning problems that highlight how autoregressive generations' performance can rapidly decay with\,increased\,task\,complexity.

papers.title: Two-Scale Latent Dynamics for Recurrent-Depth Transformers
papers.research_question: What geometry emerges when a Transformer block is looped in recurrent-depth models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that recurrent-depth transformers exhibit two-scale latent dynamics with small refinements within loops and larger drift across blocks, and proposes a second-order early-exit criterion based on acceleration that improves latency-quality trade-offs.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a geometry-first view of recurrent depth, showing that looped blocks perform local refinements and cross-block changes produce slow drift, and introduces a decoding-free, second-order exit that improves efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Loop steps shrink quickly and become more orthogonal over training, indicating fine-grained refinements.
Within looped blocks, updates are small-scale refinements, while across blocks, representations undergo larger-scale drift.
The proposed acceleration exit criterion triggers when consecutive updates stabilize, enabling earlier exits without quality loss.
Acceleration exit outperforms step-norm and KL-based exits in terms of latency and stability.
The two-scale dynamics motivate the use of curvature-based halting signals.
papers.limitation:
Evidence is observational and iteration-based rather than mechanistic.
PCA reduces geometry to 2D.
Experiments use a single GPT-2-scale model and a specific recurrence pattern.
Measurements are averaged over tokens.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models and datasets.
Learning per-block calibration for the exit rule.
Integrating geometry-aware controllers with dynamic-depth or token-level TTC strategies.
papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth transformers scale test-time compute by iterating latent computations before emitting tokens. We study the geometry of these iterates and argue for a simple, two-scale operational picture: (i) within a looped block, updates act as small-scale refinements; (ii) across consecutive blocks, states undergo a larger-scale drift. Across training, our measurements show that loop steps become smaller and increasingly orthogonal to one another, indicating better local modeling of fine structure rather than merely pushing in a single direction. These dynamics motivate an early-exit mechanism based on the model's second-order difference in step-size, which we show is superior in terms of performance, stability and time-efficiency, when compared to the KL-divergence exit strategy of Geiping et al. and its naive first-order counterpart.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space
papers.research_question: How do feed-forward network (FFN) layers in transformer-based language models contribute to the prediction construction process by updating token representations in the vocabulary space?
papers.core_contribution: FFN layers in transformers operate by applying additive updates composed of sub-updates that promote human-interpretable concepts in the vocabulary space, enabling fine-grained interpretation and practical applications like toxicity reduction and early exit.
papers.conclusion: FFN layers in transformers update predictions by promoting concepts through value vectors, providing insights for interpretability, control, and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Sub-updates from FFN layers encode human-interpretable concepts such as semantic or syntactic patterns.
FFN updates primarily promote tokens to the top of the output distribution rather than eliminating candidates.
Dominant sub-updates can signal saturation events where the top candidate is fixed early, useful for early exit prediction.
Intervening by activating specific non-toxic sub-updates can reduce toxicity in model generations by almost 50%.
Analysis of sub-updates provides a self-supervised method for early exit, saving 20% of computation on average.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on FFN layers without analyzing interplay with other components like attention-heads.
Analysis of individual value vectors may miss compositional meanings from combinations.
future_direction: Analyze interplay between FFN layers and other components like attention-heads.
Extend analysis to other types of language models or architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are at the core of modern NLP, but their internal prediction construction process is opaque and largely not understood. In this work, we make a substantial step towards unveiling this underlying prediction process, by reverse-engineering the operation of the feed-forward network (FFN) layers, one of the building blocks of transformer models. We view the token representation as a changing distribution over the vocabulary, and the output from each FFN layer as an additive update to that distribution. Then, we analyze the FFN updates in the vocabulary space, showing that each update can be decomposed to sub-updates corresponding to single FFN parameter vectors, each promoting concepts that are often human-interpretable. We then leverage these findings for controlling LM predictions, where we reduce the toxicity of GPT2 by almost 50%, and for improving computation efficiency with a simple early exit rule, saving 20% of computation on average.

papers.title: Structured World Representations in Maze-Solving Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve mazes and what internal representations do they form?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks learn linear representations of maze connectivity in their residual stream, and specific attention heads (adjacency heads) handle path-following by attending to valid neighbors.
papers.conclusion: Transformers acquire emergent linear representations of maze connectivity encoded in a single token's latent state, and their embedding layers learn spatial structure; specific attention heads are identified that respect maze topology.
papers.key_findings:
The residual stream of a single token (e.g., <PATH_START>) can be linearly decoded to reconstruct the entire maze structure.
The embedding layer learns an emergent spatial structure where distances between coordinate tokens correlate with Manhattan distances on the grid.
Specific attention heads (e.g., Layer 5, Head 3) consistently attend to tokens at path length 1 from the current position, acting as adjacency heads that respect maze topology.
The formation of linearly decodable maze representations coincides with grokking-like transitions where generalization performance improves sharply.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) but still reach the target, indicating imperfect learning of constraints.
papers.limitation:
The generalizability of findings from toy models to larger scales remains uncertain.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) even when reaching the target.
future_direction: Construct a more complete mechanistic picture of how elementary heads operate over the linear world model to form circuits for solving mazes.
Investigate the generality of emergent models by training different neural network architectures on the same tasks with different input representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer models underpin many recent advances in practical machine learning applications, yet understanding their internal behavior continues to elude researchers. Given the size and complexity of these models, forming a comprehensive picture of their inner workings remains a significant challenge. To this end, we set out to understand small transformer models in a more tractable setting: that of solving mazes. In this work, we focus on the abstractions formed by these models and find evidence for the consistent emergence of structured internal representations of maze topology and valid paths. We demonstrate this by showing that the residual stream of only a single token can be linearly decoded to faithfully reconstruct the entire maze. We also find that the learned embeddings of individual tokens have spatial structure. Furthermore, we take steps towards deciphering the circuity of path-following by identifying attention heads (dubbed $\textit{adjacency heads}$), which are implicated in finding valid subsequent tokens.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Symbol Processing for In-Context Learning in Transformer Networks
papers.research_question: How can transformers perform complex symbol processing through in-context learning? Specifically, what mechanisms enable abstract, semantics-free symbol manipulation in transformer networks?
papers.core_contribution: Develops the Transformer Production Framework (TPF) and Production System Language (PSL) to demonstrate how transformers can implement symbolic computation for in-context learning, showing Turing-universality.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers can implement symbolic computation mechanisms for in-context learning, providing insights into their capabilities and limitations, and suggests future work to extend these findings.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can perform abstract symbol processing through in-context learning by using attention and residual stream mechanisms.
The Production System Language (PSL) allows writing symbolic programs that can be compiled into transformer networks.
The Discrete-Attention-only Transformer (DAT) is a hand-programmed transformer that perfectly performs the Templatic Generation Task.
PSL is Turing universal, meaning transformers can compute any computable function.
The work addresses computability, not learnability, of symbol processing in transformers.
papers.limitation: The work addresses computability, not learnability, by transformer networks.
future_direction: Extending compositionality further in transformer networks.
Testing whether the mechanisms identified in TPF are present in trained language models.
Exploring how language-model training gives rise to such computation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive abilities in symbol processing through in-context learning (ICL). This success flies in the face of decades of critiques asserting that artificial neural networks cannot master abstract symbol manipulation. We seek to understand the mechanisms that can enable robust symbol processing in transformer networks, illuminating both the unanticipated success, and the significant limitations, of transformers in symbol processing. Borrowing insights from symbolic AI and cognitive science on the power of Production System architectures, we develop a high-level Production System Language, PSL, that allows us to write symbolic programs to do complex, abstract symbol processing, and create compilers that precisely implement PSL programs in transformer networks which are, by construction, 100% mechanistically interpretable. The work is driven by study of a purely abstract (semantics-free) symbolic task that we develop, Templatic Generation (TGT). Although developed through study of TGT, PSL is, we demonstrate, highly general: it is Turing Universal. The new type of transformer architecture that we compile from PSL programs suggests a number of paths for enhancing transformers’ capabilities at symbol processing. We note, however, that the work we report addresses computability, and not learnability, by transformer networks.

papers.title: Emergence and Effectiveness of Task Vectors in In-Context Learning: An Encoder Decoder Perspective
papers.research_question: How do transformers form task vectors during pretraining, and how does the quality of task encoding predict in-context learning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the task encoding-decoding framework and shows that transformers concurrently learn to encode latent tasks into separable representations and develop task-specific decoding algorithms during pretraining. It also introduces Task Decodability (TD) as a geometric measure that predicts in-context learning performance.
papers.conclusion: The task encoding-decoding framework provides a unifying perspective on how transformers perform in-context learning, with task decodability serving as a key predictor of performance.
papers.key_findings:
During training, task encoding and decoding emerge concurrently: as the model learns to separate representations by latent task, it also learns conditional decoding algorithms.
Task Decodability (TD) predicts ICL performance across tasks, model families, and scales.
Finetuning earlier layers improves task encoding and ICL performance more than finetuning later layers.
The quality of task encoding is causally related to ICL performance, as shown by activation patching interventions.
In-context examples, finetuning, and prompting all improve ICL performance by enhancing task encoding.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup does not encompass tasks that require multi-step reasoning.
The TD metric requires careful design of task distribution to consist of semantically similar, confusing tasks.
future_direction: Extend the framework to tasks requiring multi-step reasoning.
Apply the findings to real-world tasks.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformers exhibit adaptive learning through in-context learning (ICL), which begs the question of how. Prior works have shown that transformers represent the ICL tasks as vectors in their representations. In this paper, we leverage the encoding-decoding framework to study how transformers form task vectors during pretraining and how their task encoding quality predicts ICL task performance. On synthetic ICL tasks, we analyze the training dynamics of a small transformer and report the coupled emergence of task encoding and decoding. As the model learns to encode different latent tasks (e.g., "Finding the first noun in a sentence.") into distinct, separable representations, it concurrently builds conditional decoding algorithms and improves its ICL performance. We validate this phenomenon across pretrained models of varying scales (Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B) and over the course of pretraining in OLMo-7B. Further, we demonstrate that the quality of task encoding inferred from representations predicts ICL performance, and that, surprisingly, finetuning the earlier layers can improve the task encoding and performance more than finetuning the latter layers. Our empirical insights shed light into better understanding the success and failure modes of large language models via their representations.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers limit reasoning capabilities, and can a regularization technique prevent this collapse to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Seq-VCR, a regularization technique that prevents representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers, and shows that combining it with pause tokens improves reasoning performance without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate layer representation collapse detrimentally affects the computation of intermediate information essential for solving arithmetic reasoning tasks, and Seq-VCR enhances the model's representation capacity to improve its ability to solve these tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seq-VCR prevents representation collapse and increases entropy in intermediate transformer layers.
Seq-VCR combined with pause tokens achieves 99.5% exact match accuracy on 5x5 digit multiplication, outperforming same-size models (0%) and GPT-4 with CoT (44%).
Seq-VCR improves performance on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets.
Representation collapse is identified as a key factor limiting transformer reasoning capabilities.
Seq-VCR enables models to solve complex reasoning tasks without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.limitation: Pause tokens share the same embedding, which may limit their effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore the effect of having different embeddings per pause token.
Enhance pre-training with improved representation learning to increase model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only Transformers often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly arithmetic reasoning requiring multiple sequential operations. In this work, we identify representation collapse in the model's intermediate layers as a key factor limiting their reasoning capabilities. To address this, we propose Sequential Variance-Covariance Regularization (Seq-VCR), which enhances the entropy of intermediate representations and prevents collapse. Combined with dummy pause tokens as substitutes for chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, our method significantly improves performance in arithmetic reasoning problems. In the challenging $5 \times 5$ integer multiplication task, our approach achieves $99.5\%$ exact match accuracy, outperforming models of the same size (which yield $0\%$ accuracy) and GPT-4 with five-shot CoT prompting ($44\%$). We also demonstrate superior results on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets. Our findings highlight the importance of preventing intermediate layer representation collapse to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Transformers and show that Seq-VCR offers an effective solution without requiring explicit CoT supervision.

papers.title: The Illusion of Thinking
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using controllable puzzle environments, revealing three performance regimes based on problem complexity and a fundamental scaling limit where reasoning effort decreases beyond a critical complexity threshold despite adequate token budget.
papers.conclusion: Current Large Reasoning Models demonstrate improved performance on medium-complexity tasks but exhibit fundamental scaling limitations and complete collapse at high complexities, raising questions about their true reasoning capabilities and the need for more robust reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain problem complexities across different puzzle environments.
There exist three distinct performance regimes: low-complexity tasks where standard LLMs outperform LRMs, medium-complexity tasks where LRMs show an advantage, and high-complexity tasks where both models collapse.
LRMs exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: reasoning effort (thinking tokens) increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget.
Analysis of reasoning traces shows that in simpler problems, LRMs often identify correct solutions early but inefficiently continue exploring (overthinking), while at moderate complexity correct solutions emerge only after extensive exploration of incorrect paths.
LRMs have limitations in exact computation, failing to use explicit algorithms and reasoning inconsistently across puzzle types.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on specific puzzle environments which, while controllable, may not fully capture the breadth of real-world reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent generations of frontier language models have introduced Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes before providing answers. While these models demonstrate improved performance on reasoning benchmarks, their fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations remain insufficiently understood. Current evaluations primarily focus on established mathematical and coding benchmarks, emphasizing final answer accuracy. However, this evaluation paradigm often suffers from data contamination and does not provide insights into the reasoning traces’ structure and quality. In this work, we systematically investigate these gaps with the help of controllable puzzle environments that allow precise manipulation of compositional complexity while maintaining consistent logical structures. This setup enables the analysis of not only final answers but also the internal reasoning traces, offering insights into how LRMs “think”. Through extensive experimentation across diverse puzzles, we show that frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities. Moreover, they exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: their reasoning effort increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget. By comparing LRMs with their standard LLM counterparts under equivalent inference compute, we identify three performance regimes: (1) lowcomplexity tasks where standard models surprisingly outperform LRMs, (2) medium-complexity tasks where additional thinking in LRMs demonstrates advantage, and (3) high-complexity tasks where both models experience complete collapse. We found that LRMs have limitations in exact computation: they fail to use explicit algorithms and reason inconsistently across puzzles. We also investigate the reasoning traces in more depth, studying the patterns of explored solutions and analyzing the models’ computational behavior, shedding light on their strengths, limitations, and ultimately raising crucial questions about their true reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Self-Supervised Early Exits
papers.research_question: How can we accelerate LLM inference by using early exit heads with calibrated confidence thresholds, and how can this be extended to speculative decoding to achieve higher token acceptance rates with minimal hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a modular early exit mechanism for LLMs that uses calibrated confidence thresholds to accelerate inference, and extends it to speculative decoding with DSSD, achieving 1.66x higher token acceptance than LayerSkip with minimal tuning.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that exploiting the natural variability in token difficulty via early exits and DSSD is a promising direction for accelerating large language models in resource-constrained environments.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy is the most reliable confidence metric for early exit decisions, consistently achieving the highest AUC across model sizes.
Early exits can provide significant inference speedups, especially for larger models, while maintaining accuracy on multiple benchmarks.
The self-supervised training objective (KL divergence to the main model's output) yields the best alignment and calibration for early exit heads.
Randomly initialized early exit heads outperform heads copied from the final classification layer because they develop better uncertainty estimates and are less overconfident.
DSSD achieves 1.66x higher token acceptance than manually-tuned LayerSkip baselines, reduces wasted tokens by 14x, and exits 10.4 layers shallower on average with zero hyperparameter tuning.
papers.limitation:
Speedup gains without DSSD can remain modest when aiming to preserve the original LLM's accuracy.
Due to limited computational resources, the authors were unable to train and evaluate early exit models on the largest architectures available.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a modular approach to accelerate inference in large language models (LLMs) by adding early exit heads at intermediate transformer layers. Each head is trained in a self-supervised manner to mimic the main model's predictions, allowing computation to stop early when a calibrated confidence threshold is reached. We evaluate several confidence metrics and show that entropy provides the most reliable separation between correct and incorrect predictions.
