Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space
papers.research_question: How do feed-forward network (FFN) layers in transformer-based language models contribute to the prediction construction process by updating token representations in the vocabulary space?
papers.core_contribution: FFN layers in transformers operate by applying additive updates composed of sub-updates that promote human-interpretable concepts in the vocabulary space, enabling fine-grained interpretation and practical applications like toxicity reduction and early exit.
papers.conclusion: FFN layers in transformers update predictions by promoting concepts through value vectors, providing insights for interpretability, control, and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Sub-updates from FFN layers encode human-interpretable concepts such as semantic or syntactic patterns.
FFN updates primarily promote tokens to the top of the output distribution rather than eliminating candidates.
Dominant sub-updates can signal saturation events where the top candidate is fixed early, useful for early exit prediction.
Intervening by activating specific non-toxic sub-updates can reduce toxicity in model generations by almost 50%.
Analysis of sub-updates provides a self-supervised method for early exit, saving 20% of computation on average.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on FFN layers without analyzing interplay with other components like attention-heads.
Analysis of individual value vectors may miss compositional meanings from combinations.
future_direction: Analyze interplay between FFN layers and other components like attention-heads.
Extend analysis to other types of language models or architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are at the core of modern NLP, but their internal prediction construction process is opaque and largely not understood. In this work, we make a substantial step towards unveiling this underlying prediction process, by reverse-engineering the operation of the feed-forward network (FFN) layers, one of the building blocks of transformer models. We view the token representation as a changing distribution over the vocabulary, and the output from each FFN layer as an additive update to that distribution. Then, we analyze the FFN updates in the vocabulary space, showing that each update can be decomposed to sub-updates corresponding to single FFN parameter vectors, each promoting concepts that are often human-interpretable. We then leverage these findings for controlling LM predictions, where we reduce the toxicity of GPT2 by almost 50%, and for improving computation efficiency with a simple early exit rule, saving 20% of computation on average.

papers.title: Structured World Representations in Maze-Solving Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve mazes and what internal representations do they form?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks learn linear representations of maze connectivity in their residual stream, and specific attention heads (adjacency heads) handle path-following by attending to valid neighbors.
papers.conclusion: Transformers acquire emergent linear representations of maze connectivity encoded in a single token's latent state, and their embedding layers learn spatial structure; specific attention heads are identified that respect maze topology.
papers.key_findings:
The residual stream of a single token (e.g., <PATH_START>) can be linearly decoded to reconstruct the entire maze structure.
The embedding layer learns an emergent spatial structure where distances between coordinate tokens correlate with Manhattan distances on the grid.
Specific attention heads (e.g., Layer 5, Head 3) consistently attend to tokens at path length 1 from the current position, acting as adjacency heads that respect maze topology.
The formation of linearly decodable maze representations coincides with grokking-like transitions where generalization performance improves sharply.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) but still reach the target, indicating imperfect learning of constraints.
papers.limitation:
The generalizability of findings from toy models to larger scales remains uncertain.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) even when reaching the target.
future_direction: Construct a more complete mechanistic picture of how elementary heads operate over the linear world model to form circuits for solving mazes.
Investigate the generality of emergent models by training different neural network architectures on the same tasks with different input representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer models underpin many recent advances in practical machine learning applications, yet understanding their internal behavior continues to elude researchers. Given the size and complexity of these models, forming a comprehensive picture of their inner workings remains a significant challenge. To this end, we set out to understand small transformer models in a more tractable setting: that of solving mazes. In this work, we focus on the abstractions formed by these models and find evidence for the consistent emergence of structured internal representations of maze topology and valid paths. We demonstrate this by showing that the residual stream of only a single token can be linearly decoded to faithfully reconstruct the entire maze. We also find that the learned embeddings of individual tokens have spatial structure. Furthermore, we take steps towards deciphering the circuity of path-following by identifying attention heads (dubbed $\textit{adjacency heads}$), which are implicated in finding valid subsequent tokens.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Symbol Processing for In-Context Learning in Transformer Networks
papers.research_question: How can transformers perform complex symbol processing through in-context learning? Specifically, what mechanisms enable abstract, semantics-free symbol manipulation in transformer networks?
papers.core_contribution: Develops the Transformer Production Framework (TPF) and Production System Language (PSL) to demonstrate how transformers can implement symbolic computation for in-context learning, showing Turing-universality.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers can implement symbolic computation mechanisms for in-context learning, providing insights into their capabilities and limitations, and suggests future work to extend these findings.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can perform abstract symbol processing through in-context learning by using attention and residual stream mechanisms.
The Production System Language (PSL) allows writing symbolic programs that can be compiled into transformer networks.
The Discrete-Attention-only Transformer (DAT) is a hand-programmed transformer that perfectly performs the Templatic Generation Task.
PSL is Turing universal, meaning transformers can compute any computable function.
The work addresses computability, not learnability, of symbol processing in transformers.
papers.limitation: The work addresses computability, not learnability, by transformer networks.
future_direction: Extending compositionality further in transformer networks.
Testing whether the mechanisms identified in TPF are present in trained language models.
Exploring how language-model training gives rise to such computation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive abilities in symbol processing through in-context learning (ICL). This success flies in the face of decades of critiques asserting that artificial neural networks cannot master abstract symbol manipulation. We seek to understand the mechanisms that can enable robust symbol processing in transformer networks, illuminating both the unanticipated success, and the significant limitations, of transformers in symbol processing. Borrowing insights from symbolic AI and cognitive science on the power of Production System architectures, we develop a high-level Production System Language, PSL, that allows us to write symbolic programs to do complex, abstract symbol processing, and create compilers that precisely implement PSL programs in transformer networks which are, by construction, 100% mechanistically interpretable. The work is driven by study of a purely abstract (semantics-free) symbolic task that we develop, Templatic Generation (TGT). Although developed through study of TGT, PSL is, we demonstrate, highly general: it is Turing Universal. The new type of transformer architecture that we compile from PSL programs suggests a number of paths for enhancing transformers’ capabilities at symbol processing. We note, however, that the work we report addresses computability, and not learnability, by transformer networks.

papers.title: Emergence and Effectiveness of Task Vectors in In-Context Learning: An Encoder Decoder Perspective
papers.research_question: How do transformers form task vectors during pretraining, and how does the quality of task encoding predict in-context learning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the task encoding-decoding framework and shows that transformers concurrently learn to encode latent tasks into separable representations and develop task-specific decoding algorithms during pretraining. It also introduces Task Decodability (TD) as a geometric measure that predicts in-context learning performance.
papers.conclusion: The task encoding-decoding framework provides a unifying perspective on how transformers perform in-context learning, with task decodability serving as a key predictor of performance.
papers.key_findings:
During training, task encoding and decoding emerge concurrently: as the model learns to separate representations by latent task, it also learns conditional decoding algorithms.
Task Decodability (TD) predicts ICL performance across tasks, model families, and scales.
Finetuning earlier layers improves task encoding and ICL performance more than finetuning later layers.
The quality of task encoding is causally related to ICL performance, as shown by activation patching interventions.
In-context examples, finetuning, and prompting all improve ICL performance by enhancing task encoding.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup does not encompass tasks that require multi-step reasoning.
The TD metric requires careful design of task distribution to consist of semantically similar, confusing tasks.
future_direction: Extend the framework to tasks requiring multi-step reasoning.
Apply the findings to real-world tasks.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformers exhibit adaptive learning through in-context learning (ICL), which begs the question of how. Prior works have shown that transformers represent the ICL tasks as vectors in their representations. In this paper, we leverage the encoding-decoding framework to study how transformers form task vectors during pretraining and how their task encoding quality predicts ICL task performance. On synthetic ICL tasks, we analyze the training dynamics of a small transformer and report the coupled emergence of task encoding and decoding. As the model learns to encode different latent tasks (e.g., "Finding the first noun in a sentence.") into distinct, separable representations, it concurrently builds conditional decoding algorithms and improves its ICL performance. We validate this phenomenon across pretrained models of varying scales (Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B) and over the course of pretraining in OLMo-7B. Further, we demonstrate that the quality of task encoding inferred from representations predicts ICL performance, and that, surprisingly, finetuning the earlier layers can improve the task encoding and performance more than finetuning the latter layers. Our empirical insights shed light into better understanding the success and failure modes of large language models via their representations.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers limit reasoning capabilities, and can a regularization technique prevent this collapse to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Seq-VCR, a regularization technique that prevents representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers, and shows that combining it with pause tokens improves reasoning performance without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate layer representation collapse detrimentally affects the computation of intermediate information essential for solving arithmetic reasoning tasks, and Seq-VCR enhances the model's representation capacity to improve its ability to solve these tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seq-VCR prevents representation collapse and increases entropy in intermediate transformer layers.
Seq-VCR combined with pause tokens achieves 99.5% exact match accuracy on 5x5 digit multiplication, outperforming same-size models (0%) and GPT-4 with CoT (44%).
Seq-VCR improves performance on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets.
Representation collapse is identified as a key factor limiting transformer reasoning capabilities.
Seq-VCR enables models to solve complex reasoning tasks without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.limitation: Pause tokens share the same embedding, which may limit their effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore the effect of having different embeddings per pause token.
Enhance pre-training with improved representation learning to increase model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only Transformers often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly arithmetic reasoning requiring multiple sequential operations. In this work, we identify representation collapse in the model's intermediate layers as a key factor limiting their reasoning capabilities. To address this, we propose Sequential Variance-Covariance Regularization (Seq-VCR), which enhances the entropy of intermediate representations and prevents collapse. Combined with dummy pause tokens as substitutes for chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, our method significantly improves performance in arithmetic reasoning problems. In the challenging $5 \times 5$ integer multiplication task, our approach achieves $99.5\%$ exact match accuracy, outperforming models of the same size (which yield $0\%$ accuracy) and GPT-4 with five-shot CoT prompting ($44\%$). We also demonstrate superior results on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets. Our findings highlight the importance of preventing intermediate layer representation collapse to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Transformers and show that Seq-VCR offers an effective solution without requiring explicit CoT supervision.

papers.title: The Illusion of Thinking
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using controllable puzzle environments, revealing three performance regimes based on problem complexity and a fundamental scaling limit where reasoning effort decreases beyond a critical complexity threshold despite adequate token budget.
papers.conclusion: Current Large Reasoning Models demonstrate improved performance on medium-complexity tasks but exhibit fundamental scaling limitations and complete collapse at high complexities, raising questions about their true reasoning capabilities and the need for more robust reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain problem complexities across different puzzle environments.
There exist three distinct performance regimes: low-complexity tasks where standard LLMs outperform LRMs, medium-complexity tasks where LRMs show an advantage, and high-complexity tasks where both models collapse.
LRMs exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: reasoning effort (thinking tokens) increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget.
Analysis of reasoning traces shows that in simpler problems, LRMs often identify correct solutions early but inefficiently continue exploring (overthinking), while at moderate complexity correct solutions emerge only after extensive exploration of incorrect paths.
LRMs have limitations in exact computation, failing to use explicit algorithms and reasoning inconsistently across puzzle types.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on specific puzzle environments which, while controllable, may not fully capture the breadth of real-world reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent generations of frontier language models have introduced Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes before providing answers. While these models demonstrate improved performance on reasoning benchmarks, their fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations remain insufficiently understood. Current evaluations primarily focus on established mathematical and coding benchmarks, emphasizing final answer accuracy. However, this evaluation paradigm often suffers from data contamination and does not provide insights into the reasoning traces’ structure and quality. In this work, we systematically investigate these gaps with the help of controllable puzzle environments that allow precise manipulation of compositional complexity while maintaining consistent logical structures. This setup enables the analysis of not only final answers but also the internal reasoning traces, offering insights into how LRMs “think”. Through extensive experimentation across diverse puzzles, we show that frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities. Moreover, they exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: their reasoning effort increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget. By comparing LRMs with their standard LLM counterparts under equivalent inference compute, we identify three performance regimes: (1) lowcomplexity tasks where standard models surprisingly outperform LRMs, (2) medium-complexity tasks where additional thinking in LRMs demonstrates advantage, and (3) high-complexity tasks where both models experience complete collapse. We found that LRMs have limitations in exact computation: they fail to use explicit algorithms and reason inconsistently across puzzles. We also investigate the reasoning traces in more depth, studying the patterns of explored solutions and analyzing the models’ computational behavior, shedding light on their strengths, limitations, and ultimately raising crucial questions about their true reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Self-Supervised Early Exits
papers.research_question: How can we accelerate LLM inference by using early exit heads with calibrated confidence thresholds, and how can this be extended to speculative decoding to achieve higher token acceptance rates with minimal hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a modular early exit mechanism for LLMs that uses calibrated confidence thresholds to accelerate inference, and extends it to speculative decoding with DSSD, achieving 1.66x higher token acceptance than LayerSkip with minimal tuning.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that exploiting the natural variability in token difficulty via early exits and DSSD is a promising direction for accelerating large language models in resource-constrained environments.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy is the most reliable confidence metric for early exit decisions, consistently achieving the highest AUC across model sizes.
Early exits can provide significant inference speedups, especially for larger models, while maintaining accuracy on multiple benchmarks.
The self-supervised training objective (KL divergence to the main model's output) yields the best alignment and calibration for early exit heads.
Randomly initialized early exit heads outperform heads copied from the final classification layer because they develop better uncertainty estimates and are less overconfident.
DSSD achieves 1.66x higher token acceptance than manually-tuned LayerSkip baselines, reduces wasted tokens by 14x, and exits 10.4 layers shallower on average with zero hyperparameter tuning.
papers.limitation:
Speedup gains without DSSD can remain modest when aiming to preserve the original LLM's accuracy.
Due to limited computational resources, the authors were unable to train and evaluate early exit models on the largest architectures available.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a modular approach to accelerate inference in large language models (LLMs) by adding early exit heads at intermediate transformer layers. Each head is trained in a self-supervised manner to mimic the main model's predictions, allowing computation to stop early when a calibrated confidence threshold is reached. We evaluate several confidence metrics and show that entropy provides the most reliable separation between correct and incorrect predictions. Experiments on the Pythia model suite (70M to 2.8B parameters) demonstrate that our method significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining accuracy across multiple benchmarks. We further adapt this approach to speculative decoding, introducing Dynamic Self-Speculative Decoding (DSSD), which achieves 1.66x higher token acceptance than manually-tuned LayerSkip baselines with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms support abstract reasoning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an emergent three-stage symbolic architecture in LLMs that implements abstract reasoning via symbol abstraction heads, symbolic induction heads, and retrieval heads.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform abstract reasoning via emergent symbolic mechanisms, suggesting a resolution to the debate between symbolic and neural network approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Symbol abstraction heads in early layers convert input tokens to abstract variables based on relations.
Symbolic induction heads in intermediate layers perform sequence induction over abstract variables.
Retrieval heads in later layers retrieve the token associated with the predicted abstract variable.
These mechanisms are robust across multiple abstract reasoning tasks and model families.
Representations in these heads encode abstract variables invariant to specific tokens, and better representation correlates with correct performance.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: How do Transformers Learn Implicit Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn implicit reasoning, specifically multi-hop implicit reasoning, and what are the internal mechanisms that enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory for implicit reasoning in transformers (memorization, in-distribution generalization, cross-distribution generalization) and introduces two diagnostic tools (cross-query semantic patching, cosine-based representational lens) that link representational clustering to reasoning capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit reasoning in transformers is driven by the clustering of intermediate representations in cosine space, and generalization patterns depend on representational alignment, offering insights into the interpretability of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit reasoning emerges in three distinct stages: memorization, in-distribution generalization, and cross-distribution generalization.
Training with atomic triples accelerates learning but is not strictly necessary for in-distribution generalization.
Second-hop generalization requires query-level exposure to specific compositional structures; exposure to the same fact in other roles is insufficient.
Intermediate entity representations are located in middle layers (e.g., layer 5 at the r1 token) and are not necessarily decodable via logit lens, indicating a gap between explicit decodability and functional usage.
Successful reasoning correlates with cosine-space clustering of intermediate representations; generalization patterns depend on representational alignment driven by in-distribution supervision.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled symbolic environment, which is simpler than the rich and complex knowledge bases of real LLMs, so the findings are preliminary and may not fully explain reasoning dynamics in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can perform multi-hop reasoning implicitly -- producing correct answers without explicitly verbalizing intermediate steps -- but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we study how such implicit reasoning emerges by training transformers from scratch in a controlled symbolic environment. Our analysis reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory: early memorization, followed by in-distribution generalization, and eventually cross-distribution generalization. We find that training with atomic triples is not necessary but accelerates learning, and that second-hop generalization relies on query-level exposure to specific compositional structures. To interpret these behaviors, we introduce two diagnostic tools: cross-query semantic patching, which identifies semantically reusable intermediate representations, and a cosine-based representational lens, which reveals that successful reasoning correlates with the cosine-base clustering in hidden space. This clustering phenomenon in turn provides a coherent explanation for the behavioral dynamics observed across training, linking representational structure to reasoning capability. These findings provide new insights into the interpretability of implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs, helping to clarify how complex reasoning processes unfold internally and offering pathways to enhance the transparency of such models.

papers.title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation
papers.research_question: How can Transformers execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings? What are the expressivity and learnability properties of such positional Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces positional attention, a variant where attention weights depend only on positional encodings, and shows that positional Transformers are as expressive as parallel computational models with logarithmic depth overhead, have favorable generalization bounds, and exhibit better out-of-distribution generalization on tasks relying on positional information.
papers.conclusion: Positional attention decouples attention from input values, maintaining expressivity while offering better theoretical norm dependence and improved out-of-distribution generalization for tasks that rely on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Positional Transformers can simulate the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model with O(log n) layers, where n is the input length.
Positional Transformers have norm-based generalization bounds that remove exponential dependence on depth compared to standard Transformers, implying they can learn algorithmic tasks via empirical risk minimization.
Empirically, positional Transformers show better out-of-distribution generalization than standard Transformers on tasks where the underlying algorithmic solution relies solely on positional information.
For tasks requiring dynamic communication patterns (e.g., induction heads), positional Transformers perform poorly, likely due to the difficulty of discovering good parameters during training.
There is a trade-off: positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, which can increase sample complexity despite better dependence on parameter norms.
papers.limitation:
Simulation of standard Transformers by positional Transformers incurs an additional quadratic dependency on the number of nodes.
Positional Transformers perform poorly on tasks requiring dynamic communication, such as induction heads.
Positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, potentially increasing sample complexity.
future_direction: In-depth work within the mechanistic interpretability framework to analyze training dynamics and reasons for failure in standard Transformers.
Theoretical analysis of out-of-distribution generalization bounds for deep positional attention architectures, considering training dynamics.
Exploring the exact causes and difficulty of achieving goals like ignoring input values and preserving positional encodings in standard Transformers.
papers.abstract: There is a growing interest in the ability of neural networks to execute algorithmic tasks (e.g., arithmetic, summary statistics, and sorting). The goal of this work is to better understand the role of attention in Transformers for algorithmic execution. Its importance for algorithmic execution has been studied theoretically and empirically using parallel computational models. Notably, many parallel algorithms communicate between processors solely using positional information. Inspired by this observation, we investigate how Transformers can execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings. We prove that Transformers with positional attention (positional Transformers) maintain the same expressivity of parallel computational models, incurring a logarithmic depth cost relative to the input length. We analyze their in-distribution learnability and explore how parameter norms in positional attention affect sample complexity. Our results show that positional Transformers introduce a learning trade-off: while they exhibit better theoretical dependence on parameter norms, certain tasks may require more layers, which can, in turn, increase sample complexity. Finally, we empirically explore the out-of-distribution performance of positional Transformers and find that they perform well in tasks where their underlying algorithmic solution relies on positional information.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
papers.research_question: What is the function of feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models? The paper shows they operate as key-value memories.
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformer language models function as key-value memories, where keys capture input patterns and values represent output distributions, and the model's final output is constructed by composing and refining these memories across layers.
papers.conclusion: Feed-forward layers in transformers act as pattern-detecting key-value memories, and the model's output is gradually constructed by composing these memories within layers and refining them across layers via residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Keys in feed-forward layers correlate with human-interpretable input patterns, with lower layers capturing shallow patterns (e.g., n-grams) and upper layers capturing semantic patterns.
Values in upper layers induce distributions over the output vocabulary that correlate with the next-token distribution of the patterns in the corresponding keys.
The output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of hundreds of active memories, rarely dominated by a single memory cell.
Residual connections act as a refinement mechanism, with the feed-forward layer often vetoing the residual's top prediction to shift probability mass to other candidates.
The model's final prediction is often determined in the lower layers, with upper layers refining the confidence and occasionally changing the prediction.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to one language model and dataset, and the assumption that all layers operate in the same embedding space may not hold for lower layers.
future_direction: Investigating the transformation of embedding spaces across layers and the interplay between feed-forward and self-attention layers.
Extending the analysis to other transformer models, such as BERT encoders and neural translation models.
Exploring practical implications for interpretability methods, data privacy (e.g., membership inference), and architectural innovations.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformerbased language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.

papers.title: Router-Tuning: A Simple and Effective Approach for Enabling Dynamic-Depth in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we implement dynamic depth in transformers to reduce training costs and time, and how can we enhance model efficiency without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Router-Tuning, a method to fine-tune only lightweight routers for dynamic depth, and MindSkip, which applies dynamic depth to attention layers, achieving competitive performance with improved computational and memory efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Router-Tuning and MindSkip provide efficient methods for enabling dynamic depth in transformers, offering valuable insights for reducing computational costs in NLP applications.
papers.key_findings:
Applying dynamic depth to Attention layers preserves model performance better than applying it to MLP or entire transformer blocks.
Router-Tuning requires fine-tuning only the router parameters (less than 0.01% of total), drastically reducing training time and computational overhead.
MindSkip achieves up to 21% inference speedup and reduces KV cache memory usage while maintaining similar accuracy to the baseline.
Router-Tuning is effective with small training datasets (e.g., 5K samples) and does not require large-scale pretraining.
MindSkip dynamically skips attention layers based on input, outperforming static attention dropping under the same computation budget.
papers.limitation:
Other sophisticated training methods may exist that could further improve performance, warranting future exploration.
Experiments are limited to Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a small set of tasks due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Exploring other training methods to further improve performance.
Expanding the approach to other models and a broader range of tasks.
papers.abstract: Traditional transformer models often allocate a fixed amount of computational resources to every input token, leading to inefficient and unnecessary computation. To address this, the Mixture of Depths (MoD) was introduced to dynamically adjust the computational depth by skipping less important layers. Despite its promise, current MoD approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) _high training costs due to the need to train the entire model along with the routers that determine which layers to skip_, and (2) _the risk of performance degradation when important layers are bypassed_. In response to the first issue, we propose Router-Tuning, a method that fine-tunes only the router on a small dataset, drastically reducing the computational overhead associated with full model training. For the second challenge, we propose MindSkip, which deploys _Attention with Dynamic Depths_. This method preserves the model’s performance while significantly enhancing computational and memory efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach delivers competitive results while dramatically improving the computation efficiency, e.g., 21% speedup and only a 0.2% performance drop. The code is released at https://github.com/CASE-Lab-UMD/Router-Tuning.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers
papers.research_question: How can transformer networks be used as programmable computers to emulate complex algorithms and programs by hardcoding them with specific weights and placing them in a loop?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can be programmed to emulate a general-purpose computer by hardcoding weights and using a loop, enabling them to execute complex algorithms.
papers.conclusion: Even shallow transformers can execute full-fledged, general-purpose programs when programmed with specific weights and placed in a loop, highlighting the versatility of attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
A constant number of transformer layers (up to 13) can emulate basic computing blocks like edit operations, non-linear functions, function calls, program counters, and conditional branches.
Using these building blocks, the transformer can emulate a small instruction-set computer (like SUBLEQ/FLEQ).
The looped transformer can execute programs for a basic calculator, linear algebra operations (matrix inversion, power iteration), and in-context learning algorithms (SGD).
The depth of the transformer does not scale with the program length but only with the complexity of a single instruction.
The attention mechanism is versatile and can be used to implement these operations.
papers.limitation: The way we design our constructions shares no similarities with how real-world language models are trained.
future_direction: Further research into the potential of attention mechanisms and the ability of language models to execute algorithmic instructions.
Determining the minimal transformer network size required to perform specific algorithmic tasks.
Enhancing the capabilities of trained language models by utilizing smaller, reverse-engineered transformer networks for specific algorithmic tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a framework for using transformer networks as universal computers by programming them with specific weights and placing them in a loop. Our input sequence acts as a punchcard, consisting of instructions and memory for data read/writes. We demonstrate that a constant number of encoder layers can emulate basic computing blocks, including embedding edit operations, non-linear functions, function calls, program counters, and conditional branches. Using these building blocks, we emulate a small instruction-set computer. This allows us to map iterative algorithms to programs that can be executed by a looped, 13-layer transformer. We show how this transformer, instructed by its input, can emulate a basic calculator, a basic linear algebra library, and in-context learning algorithms that employ backpropagation. Our work highlights the versatility of the attention mechanism, and demonstrates that even shallow transformers can execute full-fledged, general-purpose programs.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: Signatures of human-like processing in Transformer forward passes
papers.research_question: Do Transformer forward passes show mechanistic signatures of human-like processing, such as competitor interference? Do dynamic measures from forward passes improve prediction of human processing indicators compared to static output measures? How does model size affect the similarity between model and human processing?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer forward passes show signatures of human-like competitor interference and two-stage processing. Dynamic measures from layer-wise computations improve the prediction of human processing indicators compared to static output measures.
papers.conclusion: The work suggests a new way of using AI models to study human cognition: not just as black boxes mapping stimuli to responses, but potentially also as explicit processing models whose internal dynamics resemble human cognitive processing.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show signs of competitor interference, with delayed decision-making and two-stage processing for items with salient intuitive answers.
Measures of layer-time dynamics (e.g., COM, TTD) improve the ability to predict human processing indicators (accuracy, response time, typing/mouse patterns) above and beyond static final-layer measures.
Larger models are not always most predictive of human processing; mid-size LMs show the strongest signs of two-stage processing.
The similarity between model and human processing appears to emerge through general-purpose objectives like next-token prediction or image recognition.
Results generalize across text and vision modalities and multiple model families.
papers.limitation: The logit lens method may be brittle, though results were qualitatively similar with the tuned lens.
future_direction: Extending the approach to more models, tasks, and modalities.
Investigating the relationship between model processing dynamics and other fine-grained human behavioral measures.
papers.abstract: Modern AI models are increasingly being used as theoretical tools to study human cognition. One dominant approach is to evaluate whether human-derived measures are predicted by a model's output: that is, the end-product of a forward pass. However, recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have begun to reveal the internal processes that give rise to model outputs, raising the question of whether models might use human-like processing strategies. Here, we investigate the relationship between real-time processing in humans and layer-time dynamics of computation in Transformers, testing 20 open-source models in 6 domains. We first explore whether forward passes show mechanistic signatures of competitor interference, taking high-level inspiration from cognitive theories. We find that models indeed appear to initially favor a competing incorrect answer in the cases where we would expect decision conflict in humans. We then systematically test whether forward-pass dynamics predict signatures of processing in humans, above and beyond properties of the model's output probability distribution. We find that dynamic measures improve prediction of human processing measures relative to static final-layer measures. Moreover, across our experiments, larger models do not always show more human-like processing patterns. Our work suggests a new way of using AI models to study human cognition: not just as a black box mapping stimuli to responses, but potentially also as explicit processing models.

papers.title: Of Non-Linearity and Commutativity in BERT
papers.research_question: How non-linear are different components of BERT, and what causes the commutativity of its layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a tool to measure non-linearity in transformers, finds that feed-forward networks are inefficient but important, and shows that skip connections induce layer commutativity in BERT.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a non-linearity measurement tool, reveals the importance of FFNs, and shows that skip connections cause layer commutativity, justifying weight-shared models.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs contain two thirds of parameters but are less impactful on performance than self-attention blocks.
The non-linearity of MLPs and SA-FF blocks follows a U-shaped pattern across layers.
BERT layers are highly commutative and can be swapped or shuffled with minimal performance loss.
Skip connections are responsible for the layer commutativity in BERT.
This commutativity explains the strong performance of weight-shared models like ALBERT.
future_direction: Further investigation of architectural elements of transformers other than self-attention.
Investigation of weight-shared architectures.
papers.abstract: In this work we provide new insights into the transformer architecture, and in particular, its best-known variant, BERT. First, we propose a method to measure the degree of non-linearity of different elements of transformers. Next, we focus our investigation on the feed-forward networks (FFN) inside transformers, which contain two thirds of the model parameters and have so far not received much attention. We find that FFNs are an inefficient yet important architectural element and that they cannot simply be replaced by attention blocks without a degradation in performance. Moreover, we study the interactions between layers in BERT and show that, while the layers exhibit some hierarchical structure, they extract features in a fuzzy manner. Our results suggest that BERT has an inductive bias towards layer commutativity, which we find is mainly due to the skip connections. This provides a justification for the strong performance of recurrent and weight-shared transformer models.

papers.title: Bottom-up Policy Optimization: Your Language Model Policy Secretly Contains Internal Policies
papers.research_question: How does internal reasoning evolve through the layers and modules of a language model, and can this understanding be used to improve reinforcement learning optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to decompose an LLM's policy into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, reveals distinct reasoning patterns across model families, and proposes a novel RL paradigm (BuPO) that optimizes these internal policies from the bottom up to improve reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that decomposing language model policies into internal components reveals systematic reasoning patterns and that bottom-up optimization of these internal policies is an effective reinforcement learning paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Language model policies can be decomposed into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, revealing distinct reasoning roles.
A universal reasoning structure exists: early layers maintain high entropy for exploration, while top layers converge to near-zero entropy for final prediction.
Qwen models exhibit a progressive, human-like reasoning pattern (Exploration-Integration-Convergence), while Llama models show abrupt convergence only in the final layers.
Optimizing internal layer policies induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to preemptively capture high-level reasoning representations.
The proposed Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO) method, which aligns internal policies early in training, outperforms conventional RL baselines on complex reasoning benchmarks.
papers.limitation: Excessive training steps for the internal policy lead to model collapse, indicating a trade-off and the need for moderate optimization.
future_direction: Understanding how internal reasoning patterns emerge remains an important direction for future work.
The selection and investigation of internal policies remain promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches treat large language models (LLMs) as a unified policy, overlooking their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we decompose the LLM-based policy into Internal Layer Policies and Internal Modular Policies via Transformer's residual stream. Our entropy analysis on internal policy reveals distinct patterns: (1) universally, policies evolve from high-entropy exploration in early layers to deterministic refinement in top layers; and (2) Qwen exhibits a progressive, human-like reasoning structure, contrasting with the abrupt final-layer convergence in Llama. Furthermore, we discover that optimizing internal layers induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to capture high-level reasoning representations early. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO), a novel RL paradigm that reconstructs the LLM's reasoning foundation from the bottom up by optimizing internal layers in early stages. Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BuPO. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/BuPO.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
